lessons.title: Components, displacement, and unit direction
lessons.objective: Distinguish points from vectors, compute two- and three-dimensional displacements and magnitudes, and normalize nonzero vectors while handling zero correctly.
scope: Cartesian components in a stated orthonormal frame
Terminal minus initial displacement; distance versus displacement
Magnitude, translated equivalent vectors, standard basis, unit direction
Zero vector has zero magnitude but no unique direction
workedExamples: Equivalent arrows translated to different origins
Zero displacement: magnitude zero and undefined unique unit direction
lessons.guided: Find a signed 3D displacement and its exact magnitude before normalizing.

interaction.purpose: Change initial and terminal planar points. Predict displacement and magnitude, then reveal a labeled arrow and equivalent component table. Translate both endpoints and explain invariance.

mistakes: Write terminal minus initial; reversing endpoints reverses the vector but preserves distance.
Square and add perpendicular components, then take the nonnegative square root.
No unique unit direction exists because the magnitude divisor is zero.
lessons.acceptance: Every checkpoint distinguishes vector components from a scalar magnitude and covers nonzero normalization plus zero-direction reasoning.

lessons.title: Vector arithmetic, resultants, and coordinate directions
lessons.objective: Combine vectors componentwise, interpret signed scaling and equilibrants, and convert between planar magnitude-direction and Cartesian components with correct quadrants.
scope: Addition, subtraction, signed scalar combinations in 2D/3D
Tip-to-tail resultants and equilibrants; magnitude of sum is not sum of magnitudes
Polar direction counterclockwise from +x in [0,360); degrees explicit
Standard-angle exact components and general atan2 direction; zero-resultant direction undefined
Active planar quarter-turn rotation in a fixed frame, distinguished from changing axes
workedExamples: (3,1)+(-1,4)=(2,5) and sqrt(29), not sum of magnitudes
Direction of (-3,-3) is 225°, not arctan ratio 45°
Rotate (2,-1) actively +90° to (1,2) and preserve norm
lessons.guided: Resolve an exact-angle force and add a Cartesian force with units.

interaction.purpose: Change two planar vectors and a signed scalar. Predict a linear combination and magnitude, then reveal tip-to-tail arrows and components. Test cancellation and explain why lengths alone cannot be added.

mistakes: Add signed components before calculating length.
Use both signs and axis cases; atan2 retains quadrant information.
Magnitude uses the absolute scale factor; the vector direction reverses.
lessons.acceptance: Independent work includes 3D combinations, a force balance, exact polar resolution, and quadrant-aware direction; zero cancellation is explicitly practiced.

lessons.title: Dot products, angles, and projections
lessons.objective: Calculate dot products, classify and measure angles between nonzero vectors, and distinguish scalar components, vector projections, and work along a displacement.
scope: Dot product is a scalar, symmetric and distributive
Signed dot product and acute/right/obtuse angle for nonzero vectors
Projection onto a nonzero target, perpendicular remainder, signed scalar component
Work F dot displacement with units and explicit constant-force model
Zero-vector angle and projection onto zero are undefined
workedExamples: (1,1) and (-1,2): acute angle despite one negative component
Projection of (2,3) onto (1,1): (5/2,5/2), signed scalar component 5/sqrt(2)
Force (-2,1) N and displacement (3,0) m: work -6 J
Angle with zero versus dot with zero; projection onto zero undefined
lessons.guided: Compute a dot product and a projection coefficient, then verify orthogonality of the remainder.

interaction.purpose: Change planar vectors and predict the dot product and projection. Reveal the projected arrow and perpendicular remainder. Test a negative projection, orthogonality, and a zero target with an explicit invalid-state message.

mistakes: Multiply matching components and sum to one scalar.
Divide by target dot target and multiply the target vector.
Use dot zero to assign angle with zero
The angle formula divides by both magnitudes.
lessons.acceptance: Checkpoint covers scalar product, angle and nonzero conditions, vector/scalar projection with orthogonal remainder, and signed work.

lessons.title: Cross products, orientation, and area
lessons.objective: Compute ordered three-dimensional cross products, verify perpendicularity, and use their direction and magnitude for area and a supplied torque model.
scope: Right-handed orthonormal frame and basis cycles
Signed determinant/component cross formula
Anticommutativity; zero cross for parallel or zero vectors
Parallelogram/triangle area and signed normal direction
Torque r cross F about a stated origin; order and N m units
No full rotational dynamics or vector-field calculus
workedExamples: i cross j=k; reversing order gives -k
Planar ordered edges (2,1,0),(1,3,0): signed z5; reverse=-5
Position (0,2,0) m with force (3,0,0) N gives torque (0,0,-6) N m
lessons.guided: Compute a planar cross product's signed z component, then distinguish that vector from positive area.

interaction.purpose: Change planar vectors embedded in 3D and swap their order. Predict signed normal and triangle area, then reveal the parallelogram with a signed normal label and numeric table. Test parallel vectors.

mistakes: Compute each cyclic component or expand the determinant with alternating signs.
Reversing cross order reverses its vector direction.
Area is the nonnegative magnitude; the normal records orientation.
lessons.acceptance: Cross answers are checked independently through antisymmetry and orthogonality. Area and torque include units and distinct scalar/vector answers.

lessons.title: Lines, planes, and coordinate systems
lessons.objective: Use vector equations to test points on lines and planes, calculate perpendicular point-plane distance, and convert simple Cartesian, cylindrical, and spherical coordinates under explicitly stated conventions.
scope: r=p+t d with d nonzero; line versus segment t interval
Plane normal n dot (r-p)=0 with n nonzero
Point-plane distance absolute residual over norm
Cylindrical (r,θ,z), r>=0, degree θ from+x toward+y
Spherical (ρ,θ,φ): ρ>=0, θ azimuth, φ from+z, x=ρsinφcosθ; singular origin and axis nonuniqueness
Coordinates describe a point; Cartesian vector components are tied to a frame; no spherical vector-basis transformations or Jacobians
workedExamples: Line through (1,2,-1) direction(2,0,1) at t3 gives(7,2,2)
Test (5,2,1) on same line, and reject inconsistent component parameters
Point on +z axis has nonunique azimuth; origin has nonunique angles
lessons.guided: Use a line parameter and a plane normal, then convert one cylindrical point.

interaction.purpose: Change a cylindrical radius, azimuth, and height. Predict Cartesian coordinates, inspect a top-down plot with a separate height table, and compare equivalent azimuths. Test r=0 and explain why azimuth becomes nonunique.

mistakes: Use a different t for each coordinate
Find one t and substitute it into every coordinate.
Treat a plane normal as a direction along the plane
Differences of plane points have zero dot product with the normal.
Read the explicit spherical convention and trace projection onto the xy plane.
Force a unique angle on an axis
Coordinates may be nonunique even when the Cartesian point is well-defined.
lessons.acceptance: Line/plane checkpoint uses shared parameters and perpendicular distance; both coordinate systems are tested with explicit conventions and singular-axis reasoning.
